Subject: Renewal — looking to stabilize pricing with a longer term

Hi Sean,

We're starting renewal discussions for our Redwood usage (annual renewal in July) and finance is pushing hard to avoid another price step-up mid-contract. Given our growth we want predictability.

Can you outline what options you have for a multi-year commitment or annual prepay that would lock pricing (or cap increases)? Specifically:
- 2- and 3-year term discounts (what % and how invoiced)
- Required ramp/usage guarantees (if any) and flexibility for usage growth
- Billing cadence: full prepay vs annual prepay vs quarterly invoicing against commitment
- Any renewal credits or true-ups if we under/over consume

Mark from procurement will own the PO side. If we can get a clear term sheet we can move this through finance quickly.

Thanks,
Danielle Brooks
Head of Platform Operations | GlowRoads

Subject: Re: Renewal — looking to stabilize pricing with a longer term

Hi Danielle — great to hear from you and thanks for the clear list. High level options that line up with what other customers doing steady growth have chosen:

1) 12-month annual prepay (payment at start of year)
   - 10% list discount vs monthly on-demand rates
   - No minimum ramp guarantee beyond committed funds; unused prepay applies as credit for next 30 days

2) 24-month term prepay (paid annually or upfront)
   - 18% discount on list for the term if paid as annual prepay; 15% if customer elects to pay 50% upfront and 50% at 12 months
   - Ramp schedule: Year 1 committed baseline = 50% of expected annual usage; Year 2 = 100% (we show tables below for true-up)
   - Quarterly usage true-ups; overage billed at committed discounted rate

3) 36-month multi-year commitment
   - 25% discount on list if paid as single upfront prepay; 20% if paid annually
   - Yearly true-ups; flexibility to shift up to +30% of committed capacity year-over-year without penalty (helps for unpredictable growth)

Operational notes: all prepay options include token-level reporting and month-by-month reconciliation. We can do quarterly invoicing against the commitment for 24/36m and keep an automatic true-up if you exceed the committed amount.

If you want, I can convert option 2 into a clean term sheet with a sample ramp and billing schedule for legal/finance review. Do you have a prefered billing cadence?

Best,
Sean Gallagher

Sean — 18% annual-pay on 24m is acceptable for this account given strategic value and retention risk; you have AE approval. A few guardrails from my side:

- Include a standard under-consumption protection: if actual usage < 80% of Year 1 committed baseline, we hold a 6-month credit cap equal to the difference. After 6 months, any remaining credit is forfeited.
- For amortization: legal will add an invoice appendix that states the customer may treat the invoice as prepaid capex for accounting purposes; Redwood recognizes revenue per ASC 606 guidance (we’ll give language but cannot alter revenue recognition practice).
- Make the +30% flexibility explicit in contract language as an optional add-on (customer must notify 30 days before year boundary).

I recommend we deliver a one-page pricing matrix (effective $/k token) and the term sheet. Ask procurement if they prefer DocuSign or a PO signature.

Marissa Cole

- 24m term, annual prepay at start of each 12-month period (option to pay 50% upfront / 50% at 12 months with slightly reduced discount)
- 18% discount on list if paid annually; 15% discount for split-pay option
- Year 1 committed baseline = 50% of forecast; Year 2 = 100% of forecast (we included a rebaseline clause after Q2 if growth deviates >25%)
- Under-consumption protection: 6-month credit escrow, forfeiture after 6 months if unused
- +30% optional bursting flexibility with 30-day notice before year change
- DocuSign link here: https://www.docusign.net/Member/PowerFormSigning.aspx?PowerFormId=abcdef-123456

If you sign before May 31 we can lock current promotion pricing and the renewal will be processed under these terms. Otherwise the standard list rates apply at renewal.
